items.title: Josiah Gluck interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, July 13, 2022
items.q: if I’m doing any number of vocalists I’ve worked with like let’s say someone like Nnenna Freelon

ctx.x: It made me think of some of the mixes — I didn’t think of it at the time — a band with a vocalist and the engineer would spend hours on getting all the levels and the sounds and the placement in the stereo field with all the instruments and they’d get this wonderful sounding thing but the vocal wasn’t there yet. And then lastly we’ll put the vocal in. And when I think back on it well there’s no room left now for the vocal. I don’t know if it’s ever done backwards, put the vocal up and form the sound around that.

Some people work that way. I kind of do both at the same time. What I’m usually listening for, and whether or not it’s with a little bit of echo or a little bit of delay, you know some people mix where it’s the band is like the straight line and then the vocalist is out front. But I try to create like a little cushion. Imagine like a little sort of pillow. I don’t know how to describe it, like that, and then the vocalist rests here. So the band sort of comes around them and you achieve that with a little bit of…

Well you speak very eloquently about your craft and art. And I appreciate your time. I think this is a really valuable session for musicians and potential engineers. And I want to thank you for your time and I hope that you land that second Emmy.
